responses.answer: This is a good strategy. EPSG:2263 is a local projected CRS for New York Long Island, so editing and distance or area checks in Lower Manhattan are more reliable than doing those operations in WGS84. EPSG:4326 is appropriate for GeoJSON because web tools expect longitude and latitude. The project should document the CRS and export transformation in metadata.
QuickOSM downloads the sidewalk and crossing data, so after export it can be treated as complete ground truth.
Those fields help users know the source and whether a feature is trustworthy. Confidence is useful when labels are ambiguous, especially for AI training data.

The answer is incomplete. A production QGIS workflow should choose official and OSM sources intentionally, set a CRS such as EPSG:2263 for local work, normalize the schema, run geometry and topology QA, mark confidence/review_status/qa_flag for uncertain features, and deliver documented outputs like a GeoPackage, GeoJSON exports, a QGIS project, and README notes.
